deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is finding the buckling load of a pinned column of length a, bending stiffness Ek², with a top load P and a uniformly distributed self-weight Q. He writes n² = Pa²/(Ek²) and m = Q/P, which is small. On the previous page the slope u = dy/dx satisfies (a+mx)u + (a³/n²)u'' = 0, i.e. u'' + (n²/a²)(1+mx/a)u = 0. In modern terms this is an Airy equation. Euler does not use Airy functions. Instead he replaces 1+mx/a by (1−mx/4a)^{−4}, which agrees to first order in m. The resulting equation u''·a²(1−mx/4a)⁴ + n²u = 0 is exactly solvable: u = C(1−mx/4a)·sin(ζ + 16an/(m(4a−mx))).

This page does the following:
(1) It differentiates the solution: du/dx = −(Cm/4a)·sin(·) + (4nC/(4a−mx))·cos(·). This is correct, since d/dx[16an/(m(4a−mx))] = 16an/(4a−mx)².
(2) It writes y = (C/4a)∫(4a−mx)·sin(·)dx, which is to be evaluated approximately.
(3) §XLI expands the phase: 16na/(m(4a−mx)) = 4n/m + nx/a + mnx²/(4a²) + O(m²). It absorbs the large constant 4n/m into θ = ζ + 4n/m. Keeping first order in m, it obtains u = C(1−mx/4a)·sin(θ+nx/a) + (mnCx²/4a²)·cos(θ+nx/a).
(4) Differentiating gives y'' = −(mC/4a)·sin + (nC/a)(1+mx/4a)·cos − (mn²Cx²/4a³)·sin. I checked this: the cos-coefficient (n/a)(1−mx/4a) + mnx/(2a²) does equal (n/a)(1+mx/4a).
(5) Boundary condition at the top: y(0)=0 forces y''(0)=0 through the once-integrated equation. This gives −(m/4)·sinθ + n·cosθ = 0, so tanθ = 4n/m.

On the next page the condition y(a)=0 gives the eigenvalue n = π − (π²−8)m/(4π). I verified this independently by a regular perturbation of u'' + n²(1+mx)u = 0 with u'(0)=0 and ∫₀¹u dx = 0. The integral of the first-order correction is −(π²−8)/(4π²), which reproduces Euler's ω exactly.

A structural remark: the factor (1−mx/4a) ≈ (1+mx/a)^{−1/4} is exactly the Liouville–Green (WKB) amplitude q^{−1/4}. The phase 16an/(m(4a−mx)), up to a constant, is the first-order approximation to ∫√q dx. Euler's substitute coefficient (linear)^{−4} is precisely the case for which the Liouville–Green form is an exact solution.
errors: The algebra on this page is correct to first order in m. The derivatives, the expansion of the phase and the condition tanθ = 4n/m all check.

Modelling issue, inherited from the previous page and not visible in this page's algebra. The integro-differential equation Ek²y'' = −Py − (Q/a)∫x dy omits the horizontal end reaction H that a pinned base must supply when the weight acts at displaced positions. The correct relation is Ek²y''' = −(P+Qx/a)y' + H with H ≠ 0. Euler's third-order equation corresponds to H = 0, and he never imposes y''(a) = 0, so his solution carries a nonzero base moment. His first-order eigenvalue n² ≈ π² − (π²−8)m/2, i.e. P + (π²−8)Q/(2π²) ≈ P + 0.095Q = π²Ek²/a², is therefore not the pinned–pinned heavy-column result. A Rayleigh quotient for the true pinned–pinned column gives P + Q/2 to first order. (The quantitative comparison is mine; my belief that Euler's heavy-column work of this period was later judged defective is from memory and unsure.)
The exactly solvable substitute is used only as a stepping stone: Euler immediately re-expands in m, so its exactness buys nothing beyond ordinary first-order perturbation theory.

ideas.what: Replacing the linear coefficient 1+mx/a by (1−mx/4a)^{−4}, which agrees to first order, so that u'' + k²(b−cx)^{−4}u = 0 becomes exactly solvable with u = (b−cx)·sin(k/(c(b−cx)))
ideas.modern_name: Comparison equation / exactly solvable potential (Liouville transformation of the form x^{-4} to constant coefficients)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Exact solvability of y'' + k²x^{−4}y = 0 is classical (Euler/Riccati era); the comparison-equation method is credited to Liouville–Green (1837) and later Langer/Olver
ideas.where_published: Possibly also in Euler's Institutiones calculi integralis discussions of special second-order linear equations; unsure

ideas.what: The approximate solution has amplitude (1+mx/a)^{−1/4} and phase ≈ ∫√(1+mx/a)·(n/a)dx
ideas.usually_credited_to: Liouville and Green (1837); Jeffreys, Wentzel, Kramers, Brillouin (1920s)

ideas.what: Expanding the phase in m, absorbing the large constant 4n/m into a new phase θ, and solving a perturbed boundary-value problem for the eigenvalue
ideas.modern_name: Regular perturbation of a Sturm–Liouville-type eigenvalue

ideas.what: Buckling of a column under its own weight plus an end load (the variable-axial-load Airy equation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (later papers, 1778, using series), Greenhill (1881) for the Bessel-function solution
ideas.where_published: E238; later Euler papers of 1778 on columns under their own weight

missed.claim: Euler's device is, in effect, a Liouville–Green (WKB) approximation 78 years before Liouville and Green. He approximates the Airy-type equation u'' + (n/a)²(1+mx/a)u = 0 by the unique type of variable coefficient, an inverse fourth power of a linear function, for which the WKB form q^{−1/4}·sin(∫√q) is exact. His amplitude (1−mx/4a) ≈ (1+mx/a)^{−1/4} and his phase is the expansion of ∫√q. I do not know of the history of WKB citing this.
missed.quote: on pourra envisager 1 + mx/a comme étant = (1 − mx/4a)^{−4} ... u = C(1 − mx/4a) sin(ζ + 16an/(m(4a − mx)))
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is an early instance of the comparison-equation idea (approximating by an exactly solvable potential whose solution has WKB form). It is relevant to the prehistory of asymptotic methods usually begun with Liouville–Green (1837).

missed.claim: Euler's first-order heavy-column correction P + (π²−8)Q/(2π²) follows correctly from his equation. That equation, however, omits the horizontal reaction, so the boundary-value problem differs from the pinned–pinned case, whose first-order result is P + Q/2. The precise source of the discrepancy (a missing H term, with a non-zero base moment) may not be spelled out in the secondary literature.
missed.quote: Mais, puisque y évanouït au cas x = 0, il faut que ddy/dx² évanouïsse aussi
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of historical interest for the evaluation of Euler's 1759 heavy-column analysis versus his later corrections; it is not of mathematical novelty.

deep.surprise_reason: The algebra is routine first-order perturbation. However, the choice of the (linear)^{-4} comparison coefficient reproduces exactly the WKB amplitude and phase, a neat proto-Liouville–Green construction that is probably not highlighted in histories of asymptotics. Its impact is limited because Euler immediately re-expands in m.
